name: Disability Tax Credit (DTC)
what: A tax credit (money off the tax you owe) for people with a serious disability that lasts a long time. For a child, getting approved is the big one. It opens the door to the Child Disability Benefit, RDSP money, and BC’s new disability supplement.
amount: For 2025, the disability amount is $10,138. Kids under 18 can add up to $5,914 more. These amounts lower the tax owed. They are not paid to you as cash. (CRA, checked 2026-10-14.)
who: Your child has a severe disability that is expected to last at least 12 months in a row.
A medical practitioner (like a doctor) fills in and signs Form T2201.
steps: Ask your child’s doctor, nurse practitioner, psychologist or speech-language pathologist to fill in Form T2201. The CRA has an online version.
Send it to the CRA with the online DTC form or by mail. Don’t use “submit documents.” You can apply any time of year.
Wait for a letter from the CRA. It says yes or no (this is called a “notice of determination”).
File your taxes every year, even if you had no income.
docs: Form T2201, with the medical part filled in
Your SIN (Social Insurance Number) and your child’s details
links: Our DTC Playbook: step-by-step, prep sheet, fees, MP help, back pay

name: Child Disability Benefit (CDB)
what: Tax-free money paid every month to families with a child under 18 who is approved for the DTC. It comes with your Canada Child Benefit payment.
amount: July 2026 to June 2027: up to $3,480 a year ($290 a month) per child. You get less if your family net income is over $82,847. (CRA, checked 2026-10-14.)
who: You get the Canada Child Benefit, or you could get it.
Your child is approved for the DTC.
steps: Get the DTC approved first.
If you already get the Canada Child Benefit, this benefit starts by itself. The CRA can pay you for this year and the 2 years before.
File your taxes every year. Both partners need to file.
docs: Your DTC approval letter
Your taxes, filed and up to date

name: RDSP, with the Canada Disability Savings Grant and Bond
what: A long-term savings account for someone approved for the DTC. It’s called a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP). The government adds money too. The grant matches what you put in. Families with low income can get the bond without putting in any money.
amount: Grant: up to $3,500 a year, and up to $70,000 in a lifetime. Bond: up to $1,000 a year, and up to $20,000 in a lifetime. You don’t have to put in money to get the bond. For 2026, you get the full bond if your family net income is $38,237 or less. When you open a plan, you may get up to $11,000 in bond for past years. (canada.ca, checked 2026-10-14.)
who: The person the account is for is approved for the DTC.
They live in Canada and have a SIN.
They are under 60 when the account is opened.
steps: Get the DTC approved.
Open an RDSP at a bank or credit union that offers them.
Ask them to apply for the grant and the bond for you.
Keep filing your taxes so the bond keeps coming.
docs: SIN for your child and for you (the parent who opens it)
DTC approval letter
ID
links: Canada.ca: How much you could get

name: BC Autism Funding (under 6, and ages 6 to 18)
gov: BC (Ministry of Children and Family Development, or MCFD)
what: Money to pay for autism therapy and support. This program ends March 31, 2027. Two new programs will replace it: the BC Children and Youth Disability Benefit (based on how much help your child needs) and the Disability Supplement (based on family income). You can still apply for Autism Funding until March 2027.
amount: Under 6: up to $22,000 a year per child. This pays for approved therapists, workers trained to help your child, and family counselling. Ages 6 to 18: up to $6,000 a year per child. Up to 20% of that can go to training, travel and equipment. New Disability Benefit: $6,500, or up to $17,000 a year, based on your child’s needs. Disability Supplement: up to $6,000 a year, based on family income. First payments start July 2027. (gov.bc.ca, checked 2026-10-14.)
who: Your child is under 19, lives in BC, and has an autism diagnosis from a qualified assessment.
For the new Disability Benefit: it’s based on how much help your child needs. Any diagnosis can count.
steps: Get a diagnosis. You can use the free public BC Autism Assessment Network or a private assessor.
Send the Autism Funding form and the diagnosis to MCFD.
Pick providers from the RASP (Registry of Autism Service Providers, BC’s list of approved therapists).
Watch your mail for a letter from the ministry about moving to the Disability Benefit.
docs: Diagnosis or assessment report
Your child’s BC Services Card (MSP)
Proof you live in BC
links: gov.bc.ca: How much funding is available
gov.bc.ca: Financial supports for children with support needs

name: At Home Program (Medical Benefits)
what: Helps kids who need a lot of help with daily life. It can cover medical equipment and supplies, orthotics (special braces or shoe inserts), hearing care, dental and eye care, therapies, and medical travel. It also covers medicines through PharmaCare Plan F. (One part, called SAET, is moving to the new Disability Benefit. The medical benefits stay.)
amount: Items are approved first, then paid for directly. There is no set dollar amount.
who: Your child is 0 to 17. Benefits last until the end of the month they turn 18.
Your child lives in BC, is on MSP (BC health insurance), and lives at home with a parent or guardian.
Your child needs full help with 3 of these 4: eating, dressing, toileting, washing. For kids under 3, a doctor confirms this.
steps: Talk to your child’s doctor or therapist.
Fill in the form (CF2160). Add an assessment of your child’s daily skills, like the Vineland-3, PEDI-CAT or GMFCS.
A regional team decides. You get a letter.
In pilot areas (Prince Rupert and Haida Gwaii, Smithers, Terrace, Kelowna), apply through a Family Connections Centre.
docs: Form CF2160
An assessment of your child’s daily skills
ID and proof you live in BC

name: Jordan's Principle
what: Helps First Nations kids get the health, social and school products, services and supports they need. It works on or off reserve. Kids should not have to wait while governments argue about who pays.
amount: Decided case by case. There is no set amount.
who: Your child is First Nations and under the age of majority (18 or 19, depending on the province). ISC has the full rules.
You live on or off reserve.
steps: Call 1-855-JP-CHILD (1-855-572-4453). It’s open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. You can also contact your regional focal point (local contact) or a service coordinator.
Get a letter of support from a health or school worker, an Elder or a Knowledge Keeper.
Send your request with your consent (your OK) and a list of costs.
Is it urgent, like a safety issue, no food, or fleeing violence? Call the line right away.
If you get a no, you can appeal (ask them to look again).
docs: Proof your child is eligible
A letter of support that explains how the request helps your child
Your consent as parent or guardian
Price quotes or a list of costs, and any assessments

name: Help for First Nations families, on and off reserve
what: On reserve, income help and assisted living come from ISC through your band office. Off reserve, First Nations families use BC programs, like disability assistance. They can also use Jordan’s Principle, FNHA health benefits (First Nations Health Authority), and Indigenous housing groups.
who: People living on reserve who need money help (On-reserve Income Assistance)
People living on reserve with a disability or long-term illness who need help with daily care that isn’t medical (Assisted Living)
steps: On reserve: start with the social development worker at your band office.
Off reserve: apply for BC programs on My Self Serve (the BC website for assistance). A Friendship Centre or BCANDS can help you.
Use Jordan’s Principle for things your child needs and can’t get.
docs: Status card, if you have one
ID, and proof of where you live and your income

name: BC Persons with Disabilities (PWD) designation
gov: BC (Ministry of Social Development and Poverty Reduction)
what: PWD is a status for adults. It gives them disability assistance. That means more money each month, a higher limit on savings, help with transportation, and health supplements (extra health help). It’s for adults, so plan ahead for your child. You can start at 17½.
amount: See the current BC rate tables on gov.bc.ca.
who: 18 or older. You can apply from 17½.
A severe physical or mental disability that is expected to last 2 years or more
Daily activities are very limited, and they need help
Income and savings are under BC’s limits
steps: Apply for assistance on My Self Serve (the BC website for assistance). Skip this step if you already get assistance.
Ask for the PWD form (HR2883).
Have the doctor or nurse practitioner and an assessor fill in their parts.
Send it in. If the answer is no, you can ask them to look again (this is called “reconsideration”). Disability Alliance BC can help.
docs: PWD form HR2883
ID, SIN, bank and income details

name: Crisis supplements and other assistance supplements
gov: BC (Ministry of Social Development and Poverty Reduction)
what: Do you get BC income, disability or hardship assistance? If an emergency puts your family’s health or safety at risk, you may get extra money. This is called a crisis supplement. It can help with things like food, shelter or clothing. BC also has help with damage deposits, a Housing Stability Supplement, and health supplements.
amount: Set by BC rules. Check the supplements page.
who: Your family gets BC income, disability or hardship assistance.
You have a sudden cost or need you can’t pay for any other way. Going without it would put health or safety at risk.
steps: Contact the ministry as soon as the emergency happens. Use My Self Serve, call, or go to an office.
Tell them what you need and why you have no other way to get it.
If the answer is no, you can ask them to look again (reconsideration).
docs: Receipts, letters or price quotes about the emergency
links: gov.bc.ca: Supplements for people on assistance

name: BC Housing Rental Assistance Program (RAP)
what: Money each month to help working families with low income pay rent. You can’t get it while you get BC income or disability assistance, because both help with housing costs.
amount: It depends on your income, rent and family size.
who: Your household income is $60,000 or less before tax.
You have at least one child who depends on you.
You don’t get BC income or disability assistance. (Exception: Medical Services Only.)
steps: Check if you qualify on BC Housing’s RAP page.
Apply online or on paper. Add proof of your income and rent.
Apply again every year.
docs: Tax notices of assessment (the letter you get from the CRA after you file)
Proof of rent

name: Canada Child Benefit and BC Family Benefit
what: Tax-free money paid every month to families with kids under 18. Both are based on your tax return. BC does not count them as income for income or disability assistance.
amount: Canada Child Benefit, July 2026 to June 2027: up to $8,157 a year per child under 6 ($679.75 a month). For ages 6 to 17, see the CRA page. BC Family Benefit, July 2026 to June 2027: up to $1,750 for your first child, $1,100 for your second, and $900 for each child after that. (Checked 2026-10-14.)
who: You live with your child and care for them, and they are under 18.
You live in Canada. For the BC Family Benefit, you also live in BC.
You and your partner file your taxes.
steps: Apply for the Canada Child Benefit when you register the birth, or in CRA My Account.
The BC Family Benefit comes by itself with the Canada Child Benefit.
File your taxes every year, even with no income.
docs: Your child’s birth registration
Your tax returns
